evidence: Draft judged: 'You may have fooled yourself in the past, and that part remembers.' against SOURCE (his own words replaced: 'Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers.'; meaning to keep, from his inner child guide: that sentence plus 'Tell me what you remember, I'm listening.' works well here.) and against the paragraph in CONTEXT. The change says it swaps only Emulate's start, keeps his ending, and leaves his next sentence alone, so I checked each of those three. Word by word: 'Maybe you've' -> 'You may have' is the same hedge at the same strength (a possibility, not an assertion); 'fooled yourself' is kept; 'before' -> 'in the past' is the same time reference (earlier occasions) and adds no date, number or event; ', and that part remembers.' is verbatim his, so the 'remembers' the first draft lost is back, and 'that part' still points at the part addressed with 'What are you protecting me from?' in the lines just before (the 'again' in 'Are you afraid I will lie to myself again?' fits the past reference). Who does what is unchanged: you fooled yourself, the part remembers. His next sentence is in CONTEXT word for word, including 'works well here.', which the first draft had lost through 'Try'. Nothing is added (no claim, condition, person or number) and nothing of his is missing. The one thing I weighed is register: 'You may have ... in the past' is a little plainer and more formal than his 'Maybe you've ... before'. That is a matter for the card (his is true, so Joel sees his own words first and can keep them), not a change of meaning. Tells in context: none PRESENT. Considered and rejected: T15 (a light paraphrase of a sentence that holds no other tell for the swap to hide, in ordinary words); T17 and T20 ('and that part remembers' is his own clause, kept; it is a specific claim about that part in a mid-paragraph sentence, neither a general principle nor a closing line); T22 (it gives the reason the part's answer 'can sting', so it is more than reassurance); T26 (remembers and remember are his own deliberate callback); T02 (the paragraph's cadence is his and unchanged by a one-for-one swap); C02 (the referent is as in his sentence); C03 (it speaks of the reader and is hedged, it is not a first-person fact about him). Lint D9 follows the source order: accepted. It is a one-sentence swap for the sentence it paraphrases, so it follows the source's order trivially, and the paragraph around it keeps its own noticing (it says why the answer can sting, then offers a line to say back), so T13 and T09 do not apply. Lint E36/E41 heavy second person: accepted. One 'You' in 12 words (8.3 per 100), lower than his own sentence, which has 'you've' once in 9 words; the guide speaks to the reader as 'you' throughout and this sentence is about the reader's own history. It reads right in its context: after 'there could be something to it', it says what that something may be.
